title: Weak robots in the plane
summary: Why the theory of robots in the plane starts from oblivious, anonymous, disoriented points; how formation problems became its testbed and the scheduler its adversary; and how a light with a few colours turned into memory, communication and a measure.

sections.heading: Why minimal robots
sections.body:
Since the work of Suzuki and Yamashita [Suzuki1999Formation], the theory of robots in the plane has asked which *minimal* assumptions let a team solve a task, rather than how a capable robot should solve it [Flocchini2023Asynchrony]. A robot is a point that repeats Look-Compute-Move cycles; it is anonymous, runs the same algorithm as everyone else, has its own coordinate system, and in the standard model OBLOT it is also oblivious and silent [Flocchini2019Synchronous]. Dieudonné, Petit and Villain state the motive plainly: "The motivation behind such a weak and unrealistic model is the study of the minimal level of ability the robots are required to have in the accomplishment of some basic cooperative tasks in a deterministic way" [Dieudonne2008Circle].

The introductions also give practical reasons. Many simple robots are cheaper and easier to extend than one strong robot [Bandettini2011Survey]; silent robots can be deployed where communication is impossible or jammed, under water or in a military setting [DiLuna2014Robots]; and robots that do not know $n$ make the system "scalable and open to robot insertions or removals" [Feletti2023Log]. Flocchini, Prencipe, Santoro and Viglietta summarise the resulting research programme: the literature has "almost exclusively focused on very simple entities operating in strong adversarial conditions", robots that are anonymous, autonomous, oblivious, disoriented and non-rigid [Flocchini2017Uniform].

sections.heading: Formation problems as the testbed
sections.body:
Almost all computability results in this model concern geometric pattern formation: the robots must reach, and stay in, a configuration similar to a given pattern [Flocchini2017Uniform]. As Flocchini et al. recount, Suzuki and Yamashita observed that whether a pattern can be formed depends on the *symmetricity* of the pattern and of the start, so the only patterns that might be formable from every start are a point and a regular polygon [Flocchini2017Uniform]. These two became the reference problems. A point is gathering: without multiplicity detection and without extra assumptions, oblivious robots cannot gather [Prencipe2007Impossibility], while with weak multiplicity detection $n \ge 3$ asynchronous robots gather from any start [Cieliebak2012Gathering]. The regular polygon is uniform circle formation. Défago and Konagaya conjectured that the last step, spreading robots evenly on a circle, has no deterministic finite-time solution; Dieudonné, Petit and Villain proved the conjecture and still formed the circle in SSYNC by another route, for $n \notin \{4, 6, 8\}$ [Dieudonne2008Circle]. In ASYNC the question stayed open until Flocchini, Prencipe, Santoro and Viglietta solved it from every start of distinct points [Flocchini2017Uniform], with the square ($n = 4$) handled in [Mamino2016Square]; they conclude that for pattern formation "asynchrony is not a computational handicap" and that chirality and rigidity are "computationally irrelevant" [Flocchini2017Uniform].

Arbitrary patterns connect formation to symmetry breaking. Flocchini, Prencipe, Santoro and Widmayer posed arbitrary pattern formation for asynchronous oblivious robots [Flocchini2008Arbitrary], and showed, as Dieudonné, Petit and Villain quote, that forming arbitrary patterns implies leader election for $n \ge 3$ [Dieudonne2010Leader]. The converse holds with chirality for $n \ge 4$ [Dieudonne2010Leader] and, after a careful re-examination of earlier proofs, without it [Cicerone2019Asynchronous]; which configurations admit a leader is characterised by Dieudonné, Levé, Petit and Villain [Dieudonne2013Geoleader]. Later formation problems change one physical assumption at a time. Mutual visibility drops the assumption, shared by all earlier models, "that visibility is unobstructed" [DiLuna2014Robots]: opaque robots must reach a position in which no three are collinear [DiLuna2017Mutual]. Pattern sequences ask the robots to form patterns one after another [Das2015Sequences].

sections.heading: The scheduler as the adversary
sections.body:
Because robots do nothing but look and move, the main adversary is time. In FSYNC all robots act in every round; in SSYNC a fair adversary picks which robots act in each round; in ASYNC each phase takes a finite but unpredictable time [Das2016Lights]. Asynchrony hurts because robots "can be seen while moving" and compute "on the base of obsolete information" [Cicerone2019Asynchronous]; Flocchini, Santoro, Sudo and Wada name as "one of the strongest debilitating effects of unrestricted asynchrony" that "a robot, when looking, cannot detect if another robot is still or moving" [Flocchini2023Asynchrony]. The adversary also chooses how far a robot moves, subject to a minimum distance $\delta$ (non-rigid moves) [Flocchini2017Uniform].

Rendezvous is the separating example: two oblivious robots meet trivially in FSYNC but cannot meet in SSYNC [Flocchini2016Constant], while $n \ge 3$ robots with multiplicity detection gather even in ASYNC [Flocchini2016Constant] [Cieliebak2012Gathering]. Between SSYNC and ASYNC lie finer schedulers, which make some of the phases atomic (LC-atomic, CM-atomic, M-atomic ASYNC), and below SSYNC lie restricted ones such as RSYNC and the sequential schedulers [Flocchini2023Asynchrony]. Weakening the adversary can be decisive: under any sequential scheduler oblivious robots form every pattern from every start, except a point, which needs weak multiplicity detection [Flocchini2026Universal].

sections.heading: Lights: a little memory and a little communication
sections.body:
The luminous model, which Das et al. attribute to a suggestion of Peleg, gives each robot a light with a constant number of colours that persists between cycles and is seen by all robots; a robot can therefore both remember and communicate a constant number of bits [Das2016Lights]. Das et al. asked what additional power "would allow the robots to overcome the inherent difficulties and weaknesses of the ASYNC setting". Their answer: with 5 colours ASYNC robots simulate any SSYNC algorithm, two robots with 4 colours meet in ASYNC, and with lights the difference between SSYNC and ASYNC disappears [Das2016Lights].

Lights then split into two capabilities. Flocchini, Santoro and Wada ask directly, "is it better to remember or to communicate?" [Flocchini2019Synchronous]. In FSTA the light is seen only by its owner (finite state, silent); in FCOM only by the others (finite communication, oblivious) [Flocchini2019Synchronous]. Flocchini, Santoro, Viglietta and Yamashita had already shown that rendezvous does not need both: either kind of constant memory suffices under suitable conditions [Flocchini2016Constant]. Under FSYNC, LUMI and FCOM are equivalent and stronger than FSTA, which is stronger than OBLOT; under SSYNC, FCOM and FSTA are incomparable [Flocchini2019Synchronous]. Under asynchrony, SSYNC is strictly stronger than ASYNC for OBLOT, FCOM and FSTA, and only LUMI removes the difference [Flocchini2023Asynchrony]. These separations mostly assume chirality and rigid moves. For two robots, LUMI, FCOM and FSTA coincide under FSYNC [Kitamura2025TwoRobot], a preprint.

sections.heading: Colours as a measure
sections.body:
Once lights were known to help, the number of colours became a resource. For two robots with full lights, the count fell from 4 [Das2016Lights] to 3, optimal for algorithms that look only at colours [Viglietta2013Rendezvous], and to 2, which is optimal, in ASYNC with non-rigid moves and arbitrary initial colours [Heriban2018Optimally]. With external lights (FCOM), 3 colours suffice in SSYNC [Flocchini2016Constant] and 2 do not [Otaka2026TwoState]; with internal lights (FSTA), 3 colours suffice in rigid SSYNC [Flocchini2016Constant] [Masuzawa2026Disorientation]. For $n \ge 3$ robots without multiplicity detection, full lights gather with 2 colours in SSYNC [Terai2023Gathering] and with 3 in ASYNC [Nakai2021Asynchronous]. Opaque robots reach mutual visibility with 2 colours in rigid SSYNC, which is optimal [DiLuna2017Mutual].

Colours are then traded against time. For uniform circle formation by opaque luminous robots in ASYNC, the time fell from $O(n)$ epochs [Feletti2023Schedulers] to $O(\log n)$ [Feletti2023Log], a time-colour trade-off was reported [Pattanayak2024TimeColor] (abstract only), and $O(1)$ epochs with $O(1)$ colours is achievable, which is optimal in both [Feletti2024Optimal]. Mutual visibility also takes $O(1)$ epochs with a constant number of colours in ASYNC [Sharma2021Constant]. With lights and a sequential scheduler, robots can form any sequence of patterns up to a length fixed by the number of colours [Feletti2026Dancing].

sections.heading: Open questions
sections.body: Whether two robots with internal lights (FSTA) can meet in ASYNC at all is open, and in rigid ASYNC the best count for external lights is 6 colours against a lower bound of 3 [Masuzawa2026Disorientation] [Otaka2026TwoState]. Whether 2 colours suffice for gathering $n \ge 3$ robots in ASYNC is open [Nakai2021Asynchronous]. For uniform circle formation, the exact number of colours for $O(1)$ time, and whether oblivious robots can do it in $O(1)$ epochs, are open [Feletti2024Optimal]. Das et al. left open whether ASYNC with lights is stronger than, or incomparable with, FSYNC without lights [Das2016Lights].
